nameStory: The Pandorus Sphinx gets its name from Pandora of Greek mythology, though the connection isn't entirely clear - perhaps it's because this beautiful moth emerges like a gift from its chrysalis. The 'sphinx' part comes from the caterpillar's habit of rearing up its front end when threatened, resembling the famous Egyptian sphinx statue.
description: The Pandorus Sphinx is a large, stunning moth with olive-green and pink coloration that looks almost tropical. Adults have a wingspan of 3-4 inches and heavy, robust bodies typical of sphinx moths. The wings show distinctive olive-green patches mixed with rosy pink and cream colors, creating an almost camouflaged appearance. Like other sphinx moths, they're strong, fast fliers often mistaken for hummingbirds when feeding at flowers.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Distinctive olive-green patches on the forewings mixed with pink and cream bands - the green areas have a soft, velvety appearance that catches light differently than the smoother pink sections

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Thick, torpedo-shaped body that feels substantial and heavy if handled, with a fuzzy texture like velvet

idTips.label: Flight Style
idTips.description: Hovers at flowers like a hummingbird with rapid wingbeats that create a low humming sound, often feeding at dusk

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Large moth with 3-4 inch wingspan - noticeably bigger than most common moths you'd see around porch lights

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Thick, club-like antennae that taper to a point, quite different from the feathery antennae of many other large moths

idTips.label: Underwing
idTips.description: Hindwings show bright pink or rose coloring that flashes when the moth is in flight, hidden when at rest

habitat: Found in woodlands, forest edges, and suburban areas with native plants throughout New England. They prefer areas with wild cherry, ash, and other deciduous trees where their caterpillars feed. Adults visit gardens with tubular flowers like petunias, honeysuckle, and native phlox.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, but peak activity starts in June. Look for fresh, vibrant specimens with unworn wing scales.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time from June through August. Adults are most active at dusk and night, visiting flowers. This is the best time to spot them hovering at garden blooms.
seasonality.fall: Flight continues into early September, but moths become less common. Late-season individuals may show more worn, faded wing patterns.
seasonality.winter: Overwintering as pupae underground. No adult activity, but you might find empty pupal cases in spring.

funFact: The caterpillars of Pandorus Sphinx moths can completely change their appearance - young ones look like bird droppings for camouflage, but older caterpillars develop huge fake 'eye spots' that make them look like a small snake when they rear up defensively!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with hummingbirds when seen hovering at flowers during daylight hours. Remember: if it lands and folds its wings, it's a moth! Other large sphinx moths in the area lack the distinctive olive-green and pink color combination.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with the mythological 'Sphinx' creature - the moth family name comes from the caterpillar's defensive posture, not the adult moth. The species name 'pandorus' is sometimes spelled 'pandora' in older references, but pandorus is the correct scientific name.
compareHints: As the only Eumorpha species regularly found in New England, compare it to other sphinx moths like the White-lined Sphinx, which has more linear white stripes, or the Hummingbird Clearwing, which has transparent wing patches. The Pandorus Sphinx's olive-green coloration is unique among New England sphinx moths.
